title: Judicial Renaissance -- Ch. 15: La Bugal B'laan v. Ramos: The Constitutionality of the Mining Law
keywords: La Bugal-B'laan Tribal Association v. Ramos
casus omisus pro omisso habendus est
primary_topics: Chapter 15 of 'Judicial Renaissance' -- CJP's thorough summary of the constitutional and legal aspects of La Bugal-B'laan Tribal Association v. Ramos, the case on the Mining Law that he had treated in lay terms in the preceding chapter and whose reversing Resolution he himself penned.

The interpretive battle over Section 2, paragraph 4 of Article XII: whether 'agreements involving either technical or financial assistance' with foreign-owned corporations exclude management and thus outlaw service contracts, or whether the word 'involving' admits everything reasonably entailed by such assistance.

The reversal of the January 27, 2004 Decision: mootness through the transfer of the WMCP FTAA to Filipino-owned Sagittarius, the decision nonetheless to rule because of paramount public interest, and the non-interference doctrine that the judiciary should not inordinately intrude on the presidential power of control.

The reconstruction of 'full control and supervision' as macro-level control -- less than dictatorial, exercised through policies, work-program approvals, safety and environmental requirements and cancellation powers -- rather than day-to-day management by the State.

The full spread of separate opinions: CJP's own original Dissent, the Vitug Separate Opinion, the Carpio and Morales dissents with his refutations, and the Tinga and Nazario concurrences, followed by the denial with finality of the second Motion for Reconsideration.
sub_topics: CJP situates the chapter as the technical companion to the preceding chapter's lay account, which was drawn from his speech at the International Mining Summit.

Factual backdrop: President Aquino's Executive Order 279 of July 25, 1987; President Ramos's approval of RA 7942 on March 3, 1995; DENR Administrative Order 96-40 issued by Secretary Victor O. Ramos; and the March 30, 1995 FTAA with WMCP covering 99,387 hectares in South Cotabato, Sultan Kudarat, Davao del Sur and North Cotabato.

The 1997 Petition for prohibition and mandamus alleging that RA 7942 let fully foreign-owned corporations exploit mineral resources contrary to Section 2 of Article XII, permitted taking without just compensation, and produced inequitable sharing of wealth.

WMC's January 23, 2001 sale of all its WMCP shares to Sagittarius Mines, a Philippine corporation at least 60 percent Filipino-owned with about 40 percent held by Australia's Indophil Resources, and the DENR secretary's December 18, 2001 approval of the transfer.

The text of Section 2 of Article XII quoted in full, with its Regalian premise, the ban on alienation, the full control and supervision clause, the co-production, joint venture and production-sharing options, and the President's FTAA power with notification to Congress.

The original Decision's dissection of the provision: retention of the Regalian doctrine, the new 'full control and supervision' sentence proceeding from jura regalia, and the conspicuous omission of the license, concession and lease proviso of the 1935 and 1973 Charters.

The four options for EDU identified by the original Decision, culminating in foreign participation subject to seven conditions -- only the President, only large-scale, only minerals, petroleum and mineral oils, conforming to law, based on real contributions, promoting local scientific resources, and notified to Congress.

The original Decision's holding that FTAAs were limited to technical or financial assistance and could not extend to management, since foreign management was 'precisely the evil' the 1987 drafters sought to eradicate, with the provision construed strictly as an exception.

The list of RA 7942 provisions struck down -- the Section 3(aq) proviso, Sections 23, 33 to 41, 56, the second and third paragraphs of Section 81, and Section 90 -- together with dependent provisions and non-conforming parts of DAO 96-40.
The nullification of the WMCP FTAA for conferring beneficial ownership through Sections 1.2, 1.3 and 11 and the enumerated rights of extraction, possession, construction, mortgage and disposal.

Justice Vitug's Separate Opinion joining the invalidation of Sections 3(aq), 35(g), (l), (m) and 56 but dissenting on the FTAA, reading the framers as barring old-regime service contracts rather than service contracts per se.

CJP's own Dissenting Opinion: the case was moot because WMCP's shares and the FTAA had passed to Filipino-owned Sagittarius, so the plea became a virtual petition for declaratory relief over which the Court had no original jurisdiction.

His merits position that 'involving' signified inclusion rather than exclusion, that the ConCom used 'service contracts' and 'technical or financial assistance' interchangeably, and that prudent large-scale lending practices necessarily entail some involvement in the borrower's management.
His proposal for an oral argument on international lending practices, and his warning that a self-made concept of strict assistance could make the country an economic isolationist.
The three issues set for Oral Argument on the Motions for Reconsideration: mootness, the propriety of ruling despite mootness, and the proper interpretation of the disputed phrase.
The non-interference policy of the reversing Resolution, with Congress reviewing FTAAs on notification and the courts reaching them only through grave abuse of discretion under Article VIII.

The mootness holding, the textual finding that nothing bars Filipino corporations from entering FTAAs, and the decision to rule anyway on grounds of paramount public interest, the uncertainty plaguing the industry and the need to avert multiplicity of suits, paraphrasing Gonzales v. Commission on Elections.

The Resolution's five-part stratification of Section 2 and its reading of 'involving' as admitting other forms of assistance, including day-to-day management, provided sovereignty and full control remain with the State.

The reality-check argument that the State cannot itself undertake large-scale EDU given humongous capital requirements and exploration risk, and the absence of any transitory provision confirming the demise of service contracts.

The reconstructed concept of control: macro-level policies, guidelines and industry standards; approval of work programs and minimum expenditure commitments; mandatory mine safety, health and environmental requirements; community development and royalties to indigenous peoples; and cancellation as penalty.
The upholding of Section 3(aq) on exploration permits, which confer only the right to explore and not to extract, with revenue possible only under a subsequent MPSA, JVA, CPA or FTAA.

The finding that the WMCP FTAA conveys no beneficial ownership and that DAO 99-56 aims at equitable sharing through a basic government share of taxes, fees and royalties plus an additional share under three optional formulas.

The excision of Section 7.9 of the WMCP FTAA, which took back the 60 percent net-revenue share granted by Section 7.7, and the invalidation of Section 7.8(e) as grossly disadvantageous unjust enrichment -- both separable from the rest of the Agreement.

The comparison showing FTAAs more advantageous to government than CPAs, JVAs and MPSAs, in which the State must ante up risk capital while management stays with the contractor, whereas under an FTAA the foreign stakeholder bears up to 100 percent of the risk of loss.

CJP's refutation of the Morales Dissent on the either-or construction, using Justice Carpio's own oral-argument point that a literal reading would force the government to deal with two contractors, and distinguishing Oposa, Tan and Ysmael as timber-license cases unlike a mining contractor who has sunk tens of millions into the ground.
His refutation of the Carpio Dissent on DAO 99-56, resting the DENR secretary's authority on the President's constitutional FTAA power and the secretary's status as alter ego.

The Epilogue of the Resolution, affirming unanimity on full State control, locating the crux in executive discretion over the government's share, invoking separation of powers, and speaking for countless future generations.

The Carpio Dissent's argument that RA 7942 waived the State's ownership rights and its duty of full control, that taxes and fees are no substitute for the owner's income, and that the WMCP FTAA gave exclusive exploitation rights and an ironclad 50-year term.

The Morales Dissent's trustee theory of government, its insistence on intergenerational real contributions, its Latin canons of construction, and its arithmetic that a contractor could reduce the government's share to 2 percent while foreigners kept 64 percent of the beneficial interest.

The Tinga Concurrence's two fundamental restrictions and five constitutional conditions, its test of whether the law and contract take away full control, and its reading of 'full' as scope rather than non-delegability.

The Nazario Concurrence's point that the rejected Davide ConCom amendment -- which would have vested governing bodies exclusively in Filipinos -- shows the framers did not bar foreign board participation, unlike the approved counterpart for educational institutions.

The denial with finality of the second Motion for Reconsideration as a rehash, and Justice Carpio's new Dissent attacking Option B of DAO 99-56 as imposing conditions historically impossible to meet, with Justice Morales insisting that economic considerations are inappropriate to constitutional adjudication.

stances.claim: The case had been rendered moot when WMC's shares in WMCP and the FTAA itself passed to Filipino-owned Sagittarius, so the plea to nullify the Mining Law became a virtual petition for declaratory relief over which the Court had no original jurisdiction.
stances.rhetorical_move: analogy to the sale of land to a foreigner who later acquires Filipino citizenship or resells to a citizen, curing the disqualification

stances.claim: The drafters' phrase 'agreements involving either technical or financial assistance' does not exclude other modes of assistance; 'involving' signifies the possible inclusion of activities reasonably related to and compatible with such assistance, including day-to-day management, provided sovereignty and full control remain with the State.
stances.rhetorical_move: verba legis textual analysis joined to ConCom deliberations showing the commissioners used 'service contracts' and 'technical or financial assistance' interchangeably

stances.claim: Insisting that the phrase means purely financial or technical assistance is tantamount to closing one's eyes to reality, because prudent lending of hundreds of millions of dollars necessarily entails involvement in the borrower's management.
stances.rhetorical_move: reality-check argument from international lending practice, reinforced by the warning that a hermetic reading would make the country an economic isolationist

stances.claim: 'Full control and supervision' cannot be read literally as State control down to the minutest details; it means macro-level control -- policies, standards, work-program approval, safety and environmental requirements and cancellation -- sufficient to direct, restrain, regulate and govern the extractive enterprises.
stances.rhetorical_move: redefinition by degree, showing that the strained literal concept would make a contractor's legitimate management impossible

stances.claim: The judiciary should not inordinately interfere in the presidential power to negotiate FTAAs; the Constitution should be read in broad, life-giving strokes rather than used to strangulate economic growth or to serve narrow, parochial interests.
stances.rhetorical_move: separation-of-powers framing elevated into an all-embracing judicial policy statement

stances.claim: Justice Morales's position that the FTAA is a mere license revocable at will, like a timber permit, would be a well-nigh confiscatory stance dismissive of the property rights of investors who have sunk tens of millions of dollars into exploration and mine development.
stances.rhetorical_move: distinguishing the cited authorities on their facts -- timber growing on the surface versus money sunk into the ground

stances.claim: Justice Carpio's dissent contends that DAO 99-56's Option B sets a 40 percent after-tax income trigger that is historically impossible to achieve, so the fiscal regime gives all mining revenues to the foreign contractor and usurps Congress's power to prescribe the terms of FTAAs.
stances.rhetorical_move: summary of a colleague's statistical case, reported at length without adoption

notable_anecdotes: CJP notes that he had initially urged the Court to dismiss the Petition for mootness, arguing a constitutional ruling should await a live case, and that he later wrote the very Resolution that reversed the original Decision on behalf of the Court.

He recounts proposing an oral argument on international lending practices so the Court could learn which FTAA provisions were realistic against international standards -- warning that closing its doors to those realities might make the country a virtual hermit.

He recalls that Justice Carpio himself, during the Oral Argument, supplied the reductio used against the Morales Dissent: a literal either-or reading would force the government to hire two separate foreign contractors for one project.

He reports that the second Motion for Reconsideration was denied with finality because it merely rehashed arguments already covered in the Resolution and the separate opinions, which together ran to several hundred pages.

He relays Justice Nazario's ConCom finding that an amendment proposed by then Commissioner Davide -- now Chief Justice -- vesting corporate governing bodies exclusively in Filipino citizens was disapproved, while a substantially similar provision for educational institutions was approved.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 15 of 'Judicial Renaissance' is Justice Panganiban's technical summary of La Bugal-B'laan Tribal Association v. Ramos, the companion to the preceding chapter's lay account. He traced the facts from President Aquino's Executive Order 279, through President Ramos's approval of RA 7942 and DENR Administrative Order 96-40, to the 1995 FTAA with Western Mining Corporation Philippines covering 99,387 hectares and the 1997 Petition alleging that fully foreign-owned corporations were being allowed to exploit minerals contrary to Section 2 of Article XII. He then set out the original Decision of January 27, 2004, which read the constitutional history from the Regalian doctrine through the concession and service-contract systems, held that FTAAs were confined to technical or financial assistance and could not extend to foreign management -- 'precisely the evil' the framers sought to eradicate -- and struck down the Section 3(aq) proviso, Sections 23, 33 to 41, 56, parts of Section 81 and Section 90, along with the WMCP FTAA for conveying beneficial ownership. He reproduced Justice Vitug's Separate Opinion and his own Dissent, in which he urged dismissal for mootness after WMC's shares and the FTAA passed to Filipino-owned Sagittarius, argued that 'involving' signified inclusion rather than exclusion, observed that the Constitutional Commission had used 'service contracts' and 'technical or financial assistance' interchangeably, and proposed an oral argument on international lending practices lest the Court make the country an economic isolationist. The reversing Resolution, which he penned, rested on the non-interference doctrine, held the case moot yet resolved it for paramount public interest, stratified Section 2 into five propositions, applied a reality check to the implausibility of State-run large-scale mining, and redefined full control and supervision as macro-level control less than dictatorial but sufficient to direct, restrain, regulate and govern the enterprises. It upheld foreign-held exploration permits, found no conveyance of beneficial ownership, excised Sections 7.9 and 7.8(e) of the WMCP FTAA as separable, and compared FTAAs favorably with co-production, joint venture and production-sharing agreements. He refuted the Morales Dissent's either-or construction and its timber-license analogy as a well-nigh confiscatory stance, defended the DENR secretary's authority against the Carpio Dissent, and quoted the Epilogue's insistence on unanimity over full State control and on justice for present and future Filipinos. He closed with the Carpio, Morales, Tinga and Nazario opinions and the denial with finality of the second Motion for Reconsideration.
